items.title: Independent contractors
items.says: An occupier is not liable for damage caused by the negligence of an independent contractor if the occupier took reasonable care in choosing the contractor and in checking the work, unless the Act provides otherwise.

source.expect: independent contractor

items.title: Grant v. Torstar Corp.
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that a plaintiff in defamation must prove that the words would tend to lower their reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person, that the words referred to the plaintiff, and that they were published to at least one other person. The defendant then must rely on a defence to escape liability.

source.expect: lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person

items.title: Defences to defamation
items.says: Where statements of fact are in issue, the usual defences are justification (the statement was substantially true) and privilege (it was made in a protected setting). Fair comment applies to opinion, and the Court added responsible communication on matters of public interest.

source.expect: the defence that the statement was substantially true

items.title: Responsible communication on matters of public interest
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada recognized a defence for publications on a matter of public interest where the publisher was diligent in trying to verify the allegation, considering the factors the Court listed.

source.expect: diligent in trying to verify the allegation

items.title: Privilege for fair and accurate reports
items.says: A fair and accurate report in a newspaper or broadcast of public proceedings, such as legislative or court proceedings, is privileged unless published with malice, as the Libel and Slander Act sets out.

source.expect: A fair and accurate report in a newspaper or in a broadcast

items.title: Slander without proof of special damage
items.says: For some kinds of spoken defamation, such as words calculated to disparage a person in their office, profession, calling, trade or business, the plaintiff does not need to prove special damage.

source.expect: calculated to disparage the plaintiff in any office

items.title: Kerr v. Baranow
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada restated the three elements of unjust enrichment: an enrichment of the defendant, a corresponding deprivation of the plaintiff, and the absence of a juristic reason for the enrichment.

source.expect: absence of a juristic reason

items.title: Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co.
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada set out the two-stage analysis of juristic reason: first whether the enrichment falls within an established category such as a contract, a gift or a legal obligation, and then whether there is another reason to deny recovery.

source.decision: Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co., 2004 SCC 25
source.expect: no juristic reason from an established category

items.title: Moore v. Sweet
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada applied the unjust enrichment framework to life insurance proceeds and explained the meaning of corresponding deprivation.

source.expect: corresponding deprivation

items.title: Conversion
items.says: Conversion is a wrongful act of dealing with another person's goods in a way that is inconsistent with that person's right of possession or ownership, such as taking, keeping or disposing of them. Liability does not depend on knowing the goods belonged to someone else.

source.decision: Boma Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 727

items.title: Recovery of personal property
items.says: A person entitled to possession of personal property that is being kept from them can claim its return and damages, and can move before trial for interim recovery.

source.expect: unlawfully detained by the defendant

items.title: Antrim Truck Centre Ltd. v. Ontario (Transportation)
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that private nuisance is an interference with the use or enjoyment of land that is both substantial and unreasonable, weighing the gravity of the harm against the usefulness of the defendant's conduct.

source.decision: Antrim Truck Centre Ltd. v. Ontario (Transportation), 2013 SCC 13
source.expect: substantial and unreasonable

items.title: Fraudulent misrepresentation (civil fraud)
items.says: Civil fraud requires a false representation by the defendant, some knowledge of its falsity (knowledge or recklessness), reliance by the plaintiff on it, and a loss caused by that reliance.

source.decision: Bruno Appliance and Furniture, Inc. v. Hryniak, 2014 SCC 8

items.title: Negligent misrepresentation
items.says: Negligent misrepresentation requires a duty of care based on a special relationship, a representation that is untrue, inaccurate or misleading, made negligently, reasonable reliance on it, and damage resulting from that reliance.

source.expect: five general requirements

items.title: Grant Thornton LLP v. New Brunswick
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that a claim is discovered when the plaintiff has actual or constructive knowledge of the material facts on which a plausible inference of liability can be drawn.

source.decision: Grant Thornton LLP v. New Brunswick, 2021 SCC 31
source.expect: plausible inference of liability

items.title: Pintea v. Johns
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada endorsed the Canadian Judicial Council's Statement of Principles on Self-represented Litigants and Accused Persons, which guides judges in making sure self-represented people understand the process.

source.expect: Statement of Principles on Self-represented Litigants

items.title: Counting time under the rules
items.says: When counting days under the rules, the first day is not counted and the last day is. Where a period is seven days or less, holidays are not counted. A deadline that falls on a holiday moves to the next day that is not a holiday.

source.expect: excluding the day on which the first event happens

items.title: Lawyer removed from the record
items.says: A lawyer who wants to stop acting for a party in a proceeding must get an order removing them from the record. After that, the party must appoint a new lawyer or say it will act in person.

source.expect: removing the lawyer from the record

items.title: Failing to follow the rules
items.says: A failure to comply with the rules is an irregularity and does not make a proceeding or step a nullity. The court can grant relief to secure the just determination of the real matters in dispute.

source.expect: is an irregularity and does not render a proceeding

items.title: Case conference and case management
items.says: In case-managed actions, a case management judge or associate judge can hold case conferences to set timetables and give directions to move the case forward.

source.expect: case conference

items.title: Evidence from a person unable to attend trial
items.says: A party who intends to introduce the evidence of a person at trial can, with leave of the court or the parties' consent, examine that person under oath before trial so the testimony is available at trial, for example where the person may be unavailable because of illness or distance.

source.expect: for the purpose of having the person's testimony available
